title: Growing a Succulent Garden
text:
My Young Succulent Garden


I was less than sixteen when I planted my first succulent garden. It was a pre-GCSE treat, an attempt to temper my (admittedly disproportionate) terror towards my approaching exams. I am an unapologetic lover of garden centres in all shapes and sizes, particularly those so large that they become their own liminal backroom-esque maze. Like cacti, succulents are an excellent present to give to a friend who can’t keep a plant alive. The clue is in the name, ‘succulent’ because parts are thick and ‘fleshy’ in order to retain water in arid climates or soil conditions. They store this water in both leaves and stems, with a water content of up to a staggering 90-95%. They are native largely to deserts or even alpine ecosystems in sandy or rocky soil and can survive off mist and dew. Therefore, they are brilliant at thriving on limited water sources, such as the once-a-year water in the novelty plant pot by the fireplace.
They have contested definitions. For horticulturalists, the term ‘succulents’ are often extended to include cacti. For botanists, it can be rather a finger and thumbs situation: cacti are succulents, but not all succulents are cacti. You get the gist. The ‘fleshy’ or swollen appearance of succulent plants is called succulence (yum), and as well as succulence, these plants often possess other water-saving features like reduced stomata (pores in the epidermis (layer of cells covering leaves, flowers, stems and roots) controlling the rate of gas exchange between the atmosphere and internal air spaces of leaves), absent or reduced leaves, waxy, hair or spiny outer surface to create a humid micro-habitat, roots near the surface of the soil, fast wound sealing and healing and water retention resistance to high temperatures. About a third of succulents can be found in South Africa, while Australia has a very low population due to frequent and lengthy droughts.
I am neither a botanist nor a horticulturist, so I will spare the long and likely inaccurate account of the approximately sixty plant families that contain succulents. I can only attest to their fun. You can see the succulent garden when it was planted above (although certainly not all of these plants are succulents, and the fossils and rocks are as much the stars of the show). It is barely recognisable almost ten years later, taken over dictator-style by the cute patch of dark green grass on the left. However, every time I go out in my garden I stare at it wistfully like a proud parent watching their children grow up.

title: Black Swan(s)
text:
Black Swan


2021, the second year of my undergraduate degree at the University of Exeter. My house is at the very end of the highstreet, almost overlooking the River Exe. If you follow the water, you will reach the quay, bracketed with craft stalls built into the landscape, restaurants and bridges and benches that in their reliable architecture hold (what felt at the time) my entire life and identity. I have recently been gifted my first DSLR, an upgrade from a bridge camera I dutifully and loyally kept safe since I was thirteen years old. I walk up and down the quay every day, often twice a day, itching for company in the tense post-lockdown months, resigned to obsessive work at my rickety wooden desk and these brief, beautiful snatches of sun in the early morning.
Black swans (cygnus atratus) are rare in the UK. In the Merlin app (my trusty ornithology buddy), it is a solid red circle (rare) and sighting one in any given area of the UK is classified as “unlikely”. Black swans are native to southeast and southwest Australia, where they gravitate to both fresh and saltwater lakes, swamps, rivers and wetlands. They are nomadic, with varying migration patterns. In terms of appearance, they are large, black-feathered birds with white flight feathers and vibrant red bills, a bright splash that would draw any wandering eye on an afternoon stroll. Across the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, they were introduced as ornamental birds in New Zealand, western Europe and Japan, with limited numbers in the US. Aside from Australia, however, their most prominent geographical association is in Dawlish, Devon. In fact, they are an established emblem of the town [https://ladysmile.co.uk/blogs/black-swans-of-dawlish-the-history-and-influence]. As such, on one routine stroll down the River Exe, I was met with a mating pair (we all deserve a holiday, right?).
After a mad dash back to my house to collect my camera, I spent at least an hour as a desperate paparazzi. Now, they remain the rarest birds (or, I would say, animal in general) that I have witnessed in the wild. I look at these pictures, and I am met not only with the beauty and majesty of their great, streamlined bodies, but a more baseline affection for both Devon and those years of mine in Exeter. I spent a lot of time photographing birds, attracted, I think, by their apparent freedom of movement. But introduction of non-native species within human-led currents is hardly freedom of movement, is it? I stood on the bank of the river and watched these birds and felt a great and affectionate calling. “We are both a little far from home, are we not?”
I had never seen black swans before, and I have not seen them since. I left Exeter and I rarely look back. However, sometimes I am looking through the thousands of photos I have taken over my life and I find these again, and for a moment I can see the crowd of them, the bright flash of red and the distinctive white stripe, and I am back there on the bank, crouching down, close enough to photograph but not to risk provoking them. Two animals facing each other off. One wild and one tame.

title: The Cure in Cardiff
text:
The Cure at Blackweir Fields
A twelve-hour round trip truly worth the exhaustion. I’ve known and loved The Cure for a very long time. There are many a childhood drive cemented in my memory with ‘Pictures of You’ playing in the background. It was only in my teenage years that I truly became a fan, largely through some of my favourite films. In Starter for Ten (2006), the comedy starring James McAvoy as Brian Jackson, a working-class university student who fulfils his lifelong ambition to compete in University Challenge, Brian’s shot of leaving home is soundtracked by ‘Boys Don’t Cry’. I first heard ‘Inbetween Days’ in Sing Street (2016), a brilliant film about a group of schoolboys who form a band in 1980s Dublin. The band constantly reinvent themselves, trying to find their own unique sound, defining their Cure era as the epitome of ‘happy sad’. I love this phrase, happy sad. I think it encapsulates so well many things in life that cannot fall easily into positive or negative emotion. It is the inevitable melancholy that accompanies major life decisions or unexpected twists. And it’s true, if The Cure are truly great at anything, its capturing what it means to be happy sad.
I jumped at the opportunity to see them live. After crossing the Prince of Wales bridge, we were immediately confronted by a never-ending queue. Eventually, after much frustration, we crawled into Cardiff, only to find half the roads in the city closed for cars, including the only entrance to our pre-paid parking. Sad. After a few clueless loops of the one-way system, we eventually found street parking, and prepared to take the financial hit and go, were pleasantly surprised that we were outside tariff times. Happy. A longer walk in the scorching sun but we made it to Blackweir fields eventually. Happy sad.
There were a few things that struck me as incredibly special about this concert. As I was standing in the packed crowd, watching people who were born decades after these songs were released crying with emotion at Robert Smith’s timeless voice, it was clear that The Cure have something rare: longevity. It was truly an intergenerational concert. I went with my dad, and families with adult children were dime a dozen. This is a band that has been shared through childhood, bonded over, soundtracked lives across generations. It’s a testament to the emotional pull and quality of the music. The set was a whopping two and a half hours (and my feet certainly felt it), but every song was worth the wait.
Onto my second point, and something that lends credibility to Smith’s longevity, is the brilliance of his voice. This is a sore spot for many singers, the inevitable decline in vocal quality as artists get older. But Smith’s voice was beautiful as ever; he sounded fantastic. I think it helps that he’s still writing and releasing music, there is no staleness here, certainly a legacy but no legacy act.
But it’s not just Smith’ s vocals that get their time to shine. As well as a long setlist, one of the best parts about this gig was the gorgeously long intros. I mean, it’s what The Cure are known for, what else would you expect? The iconic intro of ‘Pictures of You’ was cut a little, if only to make space for the numerous instrumental artistries in hits like ‘The Last Day of Summer’, ‘A Forest’, ‘A Night’, ‘The Walk’ etc. It took me a moment to realise why this stayed with me so. I think that The Cure and their popularity attests to an openness to reimagine an industry that still allows for four-minute instrumental intros in mainstream music. I think it is something that is declining in a lot of popular music, bypassed in favour of creating catchy hooks and instant gratification that can succeed in contemporary music metrics. People are far more impatient in a world of constant scrolling. A song may blow up on TikTok, but it will do so for a few bars of perfect sound clip splendour, rather than a fully crafted song. The Cure is so refreshing because you know you are listening to a world in a song, there is patience there, texture, landscape. You will be satisfied, just perhaps not straight away. There is a certain nostalgia to this, and a gravitas that is earned. For many up-and-coming artists, these approaches would be a risk. There are many brilliant experimental artists, but they’re not selling out 30,000 tickets. The Cure can be patient, they can perform at their own pace, because they’ve already cemented the pull of their music. I think this sort of patience would be a goldmine in the modern music industry.
Overall, this was a brilliant gig. The standout performances for me were of course ‘Pictures of You’, ‘Boys Don’t Cry’ and ‘Inbetween Days’, as well as a short interlude on a little penny whistle, and a truly brilliant rendition of ‘A Forest’. Even the thirty minute trudge back to the car and hours driving through an obstacle course of nocturnal animals couldn’t dampen the brilliance. It was the highest temperatures in June on record (so far) and this gig was still the hottest thing around.

title: The Borderlands
text:
In April 2026, a friend and I completed the Northumberland 250, a route around England’s northernmost county, camping between Alnwick and Hexham. We had just under five days of travel, and mid-week hit the northernmost section of the route: The Borderlands, driving in and out of England and Scotland for a good six hours of the day. Armed with an array of snacks in the back seat (think crisp multipack, crumpets and easy peelers), we took our time, stopping intermittently to take photos or film some footage of the truly awesome landscapes.
It was an entertaining game to guess if we were in England or Scotland, abandoning the map for a zig-zag magical mystery tour. The Scottish landscapes are astounding, there’s no question. Epic and wild, beautifully untamed, gorgeous streams and hills. Those characteristic English fields are far more regimented, controlled, tame. It says a lot about English tendencies, about the sort of control that the English exhibit over themselves and everyone else, the strait-laced, rod-back vision of civilisation that underlaid their imperial visions. There’s a lot here to criticise, but those farmers’ fields were also the background to my childhood, and I see a beauty in the English countryside that has been shared for centuries by artists and poets alike. That’s not to say that England doesn’t have its fair share of wilder landscapes. Just look at the Jurassic Coast, Cornish beaches, wild forests, those Northumberland wetlands. I thought it would be easy to tell the two countries apart, and in some ways it was, but in others they proved to be, along The Borderlands, almost indistinguishable.

That’s not to say that there were a few points where the swap over was decisively clear. One was the border crossing point (pictured above), alongside any entry into a Scottish village, where the flags immediately gave the country away. I’d give it to them. I’m not Scottish, but I’d put up their flag before St George’s any day. The Borderlands Day was a fun foray in the trip, although the driving certainly wasn’t for the weak of heart (although as a Devon and Cornwall honorary local I’m no coward when it comes to 60mph single track with passing places). Both Scotland and England have some beautiful sights, if you’re willing to look.

title: Elan Valley
text:
Elan Valley, Wales


In March of 2025, I visited Wales for a few nights with one of my closest friends. We had discovered a dream BnB a year before while attending the Hay Festival at Hay-on-Wye: a love letter to the world’s unapologetic book nerds. Both employed, rolling in our minimally disposable cash, we planned a trip of beautiful breakfasts, gentle strolls through the countryside and a few tasteful hours lying in bed watching every Night at the Museum. The highlight of our trip however, and almost entirely unexpected, was the six hours we got totally lost while “hiking” the stunning Elan Valley.
We started with a reasonable stroll through an established path, where I was stuck with boundless enthusiasm to the “record” function of the Merlin app. Itching for a little more adventure, we went off path, encouraged by passers-by that the loop lasted only an hour or two, and that we were, seemingly at every point “nearly there”. We had no water, no snacks (travesty!) and no signal, so for the following six hours, we were wandering about in the hope that we were travelling somewhat in the right direction of the car park. I do have to confess that my survival skills are minimal (something that I plan to rectify in the coming years) and there was one stretch of A-road with no signal that almost sent me spiralling. We met gaggles of watchful rams and a group of four boys who led us through (our Hobbit savours), a red kite and some of the most beautiful sights I have seen in Britain. I remember often the farm we passed that carried such a malevolent energy that the crazed barking still visits me in my sleep. I often have dreams that involve farms and fearful feeling. One, which I must have had when I was fifteen or younger, was simply a soundtrack of squealing pigs being slaughtered. Anyway, I digress.
Back to civilisation, we got a great curry and slathered our blisters in antiseptic. Elan Valley remains a very fond memory, for the spontaneous “hike”, the hilarious antics, and even the inconsistent but imposing sense of dread. I would certainly go back at the earliest opportunity. I would even get lost again. Some better shoes and a packet of biscuits, then send me on my way.

title: Port Eynon
text:
Port Eynon
On my first morning in Port Eynon, I wake almost with the dawn. I have slept like the dead, but the gaps in my curtains have cast a cold morning light onto my face, and my body has decided that this alarm is primal and unignorable. Although the room is new, the house I am staying in has the warm familiarity of a holiday home, a place I have stayed in for the last three years. I know the shape of the rooms and the furniture like I am returning to an old house I once lived in as a student. It is comparable aside from the fact that here, nothing changes, not the upholstery on the sofa cushions or the wooden bench in the back garden.
From the house, I can walk less than five minutes to the tide, over dunes broken only by a stable wooden path buried under a thin layer of sand. The tide is low, far out across the vast expanse of beach. To the right, you can see the rocks that stretch into the sea, but here, where I am swimming, it is perfectly sandy. There are beautiful rivulets in the sand where the tide has retreated in the early morning, leaving behind the occasional limpet or string of seaweed. In the water, the waves are practically non-existent, and it is so clear that I can see beneath my feet shoals of tiny fish and crabs skuttling across the sea floor in the intricate spiralled shells of their home. If I look to the rocks spread across the sands and the cliffs overhanging them, the ocean shivers like grains of sand against one another, but turning back towards the sun I am met with a blank sheet of white, squinting against the light which wields itself like a scythe. I know that from the balcony of the house, the endless stretch of water will take on the appearance of glittered starlight, winking apparitions against the ghostly silhouette of Devon, sitting beneath the stringy clouds.

Along the Shore
Port Eynon is a small village with a couple of fish and chip shops, a gift shop and two pubs. It is clear from the moment you arrive that you have stepped into a community. When the holidaymakers depart at the end of August, you feel almost certain that the pubs will still hold their social buzz on a Saturday evening, that the beach will still witness the exited thump of dog paws in the early morning sun. I swim in Port Eynon Bay, and Port Eynon Point, which is just besides, is the most southerly point in the Gower Peninsula. Just past the caravan park, you can find the derelict ‘salt house’ which was used for extracting salt from sea water, up to the mid-19th century. If you scramble up a little further and fight your way through the ferns like a traveller with need of a panga in the rainforest, you can reach the edge of the cliff, a fantastic place to view the sunset.

A Port Eynon Sunset
In the sea, the peaceful water is disturbed. I am up to my shoulders, still shivering as I attempt to acclimatise with the cold. It is a dolphin, then a pod. Their streamlined bodies move further out from the shore, but I still see a pair leap and disappear again. It is early enough that I am almost entirely alone, but there is still a fellow swimmer who I can exclaim to. Although I am notoriously hostile towards dolphins, the experience of seeing them for myself, so unexpectantly and intimately, produces an unexpected wonder. A beautiful beach, comparatively calm to the Mumbles, thirty minutes through winding roads to the edge of Swansea, Port Eynon is a familiar and adored stretch of coastline in the Gower.

title: Stave Churches in Norway
text:
Stave Church


In January of 2024, I travelled to Norway to stay at my friend’s cabin, and ski for the first time. We met while she was studying abroad in London and have since taken turns to show each other some of the dear and wonderful parts of our respective countries. We stayed a few hours from Oslo, and drove back in the chilling winter snow, my toes perpetually numb, every moment outside marked by the feeling of frost coating the inside of my nostrils. We saw great stone trolls, sweeping snowy roads, dense fir forests, and through the blanket of white, the unique, awesome spires of Norway’s surviving stave churches. Only 28 stave churches remain standing in Norway, constructed from wood, largely built between 1150 and 1350. They are common in high valleys and forest land, where the areas are less populated. While hundreds of stave churches were originally built, the majority have been destroyed through redesign, conversion, dismantlement or natural disasters like fires, storms or avalanches.
We couldn’t stay outside for long. A true Brit, even my warmest clothes were unequipped for the Norway cold. However, these great and beautiful buildings stick in my mind. I am always fond of a spire, tied as I am to the welcoming beacon of home that is the spire of Salisbury cathedral, the rich maroon against the stark white snow, the peaking headstones, the elegant and neat wood. On the same drive, we saw a moose. I have never been to Vermont, but I listen to Noah Kahan every time I set food in Norway, and when I get home, I’m always Homesick for a country that’s not my own.

title: An Introduction to My Thesis
text:
My Family in Uganda
I fell into history quite by chance. It was the product of an incremental tightening of my academic options, from GCSE to A Level, picked for an undergraduate degree for fickle reasons, and then adopted with an open-eyed curiosity, and later, a tentative love. It is difficult not to be appreciative of the type of history I specialise in. Indeed, I am a product of it. In short, my research is focused on collective memory and place-making among British Ugandan Asians from 1972 to the present day. I was introduced to this period of history from birth. My father is a Ugandan Asian, my family are Ugandan Asians, and I have grown up with a quiet appreciation and curiosity not only for their personal story of displacement and resettlement, but also for the wider currents of postcolonial mentalities in a decolonising world. I’m intending here to make the current direction of my thesis simple and to outline the directions I intend to take across the course of my PhD at the University of Cambridge.

title: An Introduction to My Thesis
text:
The Context: Asians in Uganda
My project in theory starts at the point of Ugandan Asians entering Britain in 1972. A military dictator called Idi Amin (or, if you would like to refer to him by his full self-appointed title, His Excellency, President for Life, Field Marshal Al Hadji Doctor Idi Amin Dada, VC, DSO, MC, CBE, Lord of All the Beasts of the Earth and Fishes of the Seas and Conqueror of the British Empire in Africa in General and Uganda in Particular), expelled the Asian population from Uganda, giving them 90 days to leave the country. However, to understand this pivotal event, we must look backwards to the colonial period in East Africa and the wider legacies of the British Empire globally.
During the colonial period, there was significant migration from the Indian subcontinent to East African colonies, including Uganda. These migrants were not only indentured labourers, but also merchants, traders and civil servants. In colonial Uganda, British imperialist and divide-and-rule tactics created a tripartite social structure, which encouraged Ugandan Asians to separate themselves from the African population, developing a colonial ‘sandwich’ which situated the Asian population above Black Africans and below white Europeans. Although these structures could blur and shift, the majority of interactions between Asians and Africans occurred in a commercial context, through trade and marketplace interaction. This created an intersection of race and class which became politicised, and built resentment towards this Asian minority, who in the eyes of many Black Africans, fulfilled roles of ‘sub-imperialists’.
Following Ugandan independence in 1962, this separation continued into the postcolonial state. Many Ugandan Asians chose to retain the British citizenship they had acquired during empire rather than take Ugandan citizenship, contributing to accusations of lack of national loyalty. The Asian population became the target of significant criticisms, particularly surrounding their lack of meaningful social interaction with Africans, refusal to intermarry and ‘exploitative’ economic practices. Across postindependence Africa, including East African states, ‘Africanisation’ policies were enacted to regain control over the economy and facilitate national autonomy. These policies led to a small but significant migration of Asians from Uganda and Kenya. When I first came to study this period of history, my research was focused on race relations in postcolonial Uganda, mainly how this colonial racial hierarchy (and subsequent changing perceptions of race upon the move to Britain) impacted how Ugandan Asians interacted with Ugandan Africans.

title: An Introduction to My Thesis
section: The Expulsion: Ugandan Asians Come to Britain
text:
The Expulsion: Ugandan Asians Come to Britain
In 1971, Idi Amin staged a coup against the president of Uganda, Milton Obote, seizing control of the country. Amin was particularly vocal about his distrust of the Asian community and their ‘exploitative’ and ‘exclusive’ presence in Uganda. In 1972, he announced an expulsion decree, aimed primarily at non-Ugandan passport holding Asians. What followed was a mass exodus of over 50,000 Ugandan Asians, many of whom came to Britain due to their status as UKPHs. The expulsion as a pivotal event is well-explored in both public history and academic scholarship. It is important to highlight here the drastic difference in not only the material conditions of life in Uganda and Britain, but also the alternative racial structures, social expectations and emotional experiences. I consider the expulsion a ‘rupture’ event, a clear divide between before and after.
My project is concerned with the Britain which Ugandan Asians entered. It was, to put it lightly, hostile. A series of immigration acts from the 1960s aimed to restrict the entry of non-white immigrants, particularly former colonial subjects, into the UK. Pervasive fears around the loss of white British culture were compounded by the fearmongering anti-immigration stances of politicians like Enoch Powell. Although Britain had an obligation to accept the UKPHing British Ugandan Asians under international law, the former colonial metropole tried their hardest to shift the burden onto the international community, by spinning the resettlement of Ugandan Asians from a legal obligation to a ‘humanitarian’ refugee crisis. The Uganda Resettlement Board, which was established to manage the influx of Ugandan Asians, therefore conducted the task of rehousing and resettling thousands of families within this fragile and hostile environment.
What followed was an unofficial ‘dispersal’ policy, which divided the country into ‘red’ and ‘green’ areas. Red areas were anywhere where the board deemed resettlement would be undesirable: either due to pressure on council services or because there was already a preexisting Asian community, which would fan fears of non-white immigrant ‘takeovers’. These included many areas in London and also Leicester (who actually put out official advertisements in the Ugandan Argus, a Ugandan newspaper, to warn Ugandan Asians not to come to the city) as well as other, primarily urban, environments. ‘Green’ areas were usually counties with a smaller non-white population, more rural, and without any preexisting cultural or social structures to enable Ugandan Asians to resettle and integrate.

title: An Introduction to My Thesis
section: The Project: Intergenerational Memory, Place-Making and Race in 1970s Britain
text:
The Project: Intergenerational Memory, Place-Making and Race in 1970s Britain
To explore the experiences of Ugandan Asians in Britain, I grapple with the collision of Uganda and Britain, colonial and metropole, while focusing on the intricacies of establishing place and community for migrant families. This is concerned not only with Ugandan Asians in white, British spaces, but also the establishment of uniquely Ugandan Asian spaces through interactions with other ethnic minority groups. I conceptualise ‘space’ and ‘place’ as conscious sites of meaning, exploring how community and identity were filtered through not only emotional and mental frames but also physical structures, such as community centres and religious institutions. Turning to broader intergenerational explorations, I employ two main threads of interest: Ugandan Asians as ‘categories of the state’, and commemorative practices. To examine Ugandan Asians as ‘categories of the state’ I interrogate the ‘success narrative’ built around Ugandan Asians, which presented them as ‘good’, educated and hardworking immigrants who would successfully integrate. Situated within the context of methods of imperial control, this narrative was utilised by the media to mitigate anti-immigration fears and subsequently benefitted the aims of the URB and British government. It is with commemorative practices that the spatial lens becomes paramount, where commemoration is used as a conscious and purposeful tool of community, memory and identity formation. Within this, I explore Ugandan Asian articulation and rearticulation of historical experience as a means of self-identification and collective community building. Essentially, I consider commemorative events, particularly those focused on anniversaries of the expulsion, as sources within their own right. How do these commemorations attest to the feeling of belonging in Britain, of making ‘space’ for migrant experience? What do they say about the roots of Ugandan Asian memory, where the focus is often centred more around 1972 as a historical pivot, rather than on longer processes of diasporic migration?
My central source base will be a collection of oral interviews. I’m not only concerned with what happened in the past, but more crucially how the past is experienced, used as a tool for ongoing identity construction and collectively remembered, or misremembered. The power dynamics inherent to the articulation, recovery and exploration of memory operate within a spatial framework. As such, spatiality as a theoretical model is needed not only as a tool for the examination of Ugandan Asian place-making, but also as a consideration in memory studies. It differentiates ‘space’ from ‘place’, with the latter representing physical spaces that have been naturalised through patterns, behaviour and communications, or more simply, created through the act of naming and imbuing with meaning. ‘Place-making’ is concerned with the conscious creation of place to serve the needs of individuals or communities, in my case to create and articulate a sense of Ugandan Asian belonging within Britain. I take these theoretical underpinnings to form a methodological basis through which I can gain a greater understanding of the day-to-day constructions of ‘space’ and ‘place’ with which Ugandan Asians negotiated their lives in Britain. Oral history, as a way of engaging with cultural memory, can be understood as a conversation between representations of the past and symbolic representations available in the present. The practice of oral history, therefore, is not about simply witnessing a participant articulate the past, but rather it is a unique form of knowledge production that is based on the exchange between myself as the interviewer and my participant. I therefore engage with ‘space’ on two levels: a historical understanding of how Ugandan Asians have negotiated spaces in Britain from 1972 to the present day, and how the space of the oral history interview shapes the creation of historical knowledge in the present moment.
This project is one which has a lot to say to ideas of race in postimperial Britain. It intervenes in a fast-changing academic landscape which is concerned with understanding the racialised nature of 1970s Britain as a reaction to the winding up of empire. This period saw a bifurcated system (meaning forked into two separate branches) with harsh external immigration laws and emerging focus on multiculturalism, pluralism and broad citizenship rights within the country. The best way to see this is like a cream egg (hard exterior and gooey interior). This period of British history therefore lies in a longer process of imperial logics and governance. It is also interested in diasporic identities, the way the category of the ‘refugee’ was formed, and how migrant groups perceive themselves and their position in host countries. It’s a project that can only be viewed from the present moment, a history that is still very much alive and kicking.

title: Sounds of the Summer
text: A collection of songs for the summer, temporally collected from near and far. Those from far are capturing nostalgia largely, of younger summers and gentler days. There is very little that is gentle about this summer, one so putridly hot that my skin has been melting since June, and I am more aware than ever of the impending climate catastrophe that we are rubbing shoulders with: a decline of our own design. I think it is fair to say that I am not a summer person, much preferring the cool of Autumn or blossoming possibility of Spring, but in these songs I try to anchor a particular feeling, of a break from the mundane, the long summer holidays during schooltime, or the briefly captured week of annual leave in mid-August.

title: Sounds of the Summer
text:
‘Alive’ – Empire of the Sun
The most recent addition on my list, this is a song for the peak of carefree summer days. As with the majority of these songs, it’s a windows down, hair flying, letting go sort of wonder. On the flip-side, I also think it captures for me a certain type of mania, of marching into the abyss with a heavy beat and a beaming smile.

title: Sounds of the Summer
text:
‘She’s Casual’ – The Hunna
A purely nostalgic song, this is the sound of seventeen to me. I associate this song largely with summers in Cornwall, walking along the breakwater and quiet canals before packing up my clothes for a trip to a local festival. It starts with a soft introduction and leaps into a crazy, heart-bending summer anthem.

title: Sounds of the Summer
text:
‘What For’ – Sea Girls
It’s not totally accurate for me to call this a summer song. It followed me through several years of my teenagerhood and is one of the earliest singles by the indie-rock band Sea Girls. Sea Girls are my ‘I knew them before I was famous’ moment, as a huge fan since sixteen, I have followed their output from their earliest EPs. I chose this song for the list because it evokes the feeling of a relentless sun on your face, almost running like a live performance, as if you are listening from the pit at a festival, surviving purely off stall-bought noodles and water from the fountain by the toilets.

title: Sounds of the Summer
text:
‘Cough Syrup’ – Young the Giant
The day is coming to a close, the heat dissipating, and this song is playing through some tinny speakers on the cooling sand. You have a can of cider in one hand and the swathes of the ocean in front of you. As you listen, you become perpetually seventeen.

title: Sounds of the Summer
text:
‘Bad Guys Always Win’ – Circa Waves
I associate this fast-paced, dizzy song with early summer days in Wales, staying in a bed and breakfast, waking each day to the eager sun crawling its way underneath the curtains. It’s a short and snappy track on Circa Waves’ Death & Love. Overall, this entire album is a slice of summer for me, largely for periods of intense listening in the early summer months. Unlike some of the songs on this list, that for me capture the high days of heat in July or the slow decay of green that heralds the beginning of Autumn, this is a song for the start of summer, when Spring gives way and collapses into endless open fields.

title: Sounds of the Summer
text:
‘Feeding Line’ – Boy & Bear
Another track for a late evening walk, when the days are at their longest and it doesn’t get dark until ten. This song has been floating around my head for a while, linked to the endless paths around my house, the grassy verges leaking their green in the heat, the fields wrapped up and pressed into neat hay bales, the wizening trees and sweating, burning sky. It’s my walk home from school and my post-university nature loop.

title: Sounds of the Summer
section: ‘Girls Like You’ – The Naked and Famous
text:
‘Girls Like You’ – The Naked and Famous
You have to commit to this song. It’s a bit on the longer side, walking steadily with an almost pestering consistency, before it leaps seamlessly to suffocating, tantalising rhythm. Whenever I listen to this song, I feel as if I am trapped inside an American blockbuster, at the edge of a canyon or over a vast lake, young and carefree, my whole life whittled down to those moments of childish wonder. With a long outro, the day in time fades away, and you are left to ponder the fleeting intensity of your youth.

title: Sounds of the Summer
text:
‘Inbetween Days’ – The Cure
A classic for a reason, the soundtrack to a coming-of-age film, a great song for the train (from which I am writing this now), where you can watch the endless English fields sprint past you with magnetising sharpness, like light from the slats of your blinds.

title: Sounds of the Summer
text:
‘Getaway’ – Blossoms
A hypnotic summer beat, the sort of song you can play when you are getting ready in the morning for a day in the lethargic sun. Once again, this is a song pulled from my youth. There is certainly a melancholy underneath the upbeat rhythm, one which I can align with the feeling of time running slowly away from you, and the cold of autumn bracing for your impact.

title: Sounds of the Summer
text:
‘I Dare You’ – The Regrettes
Completely feel-good fun. I have loved this song for a while, and it captures for me the heady abandon that accompanies having a summer crush or even falling in love. The Regrettes have a knack for this kind of music, as if you stumble on the diary of an energetic young woman who has an unquenchable lust for life. It’s great music to listen to when you need an emotional pick-me-up.

title: Sounds of the Summer
text:
‘Riptide’ – Vance Joy
The quintessential summer song, only slightly dampened by its constant replay value in retail corporate playlists. There is a certain freedom to this undeniable hit, a sense of possibility that got me through many tough days working in retail. It was the song that came on and lifted a little of the white-light headache and customer service fatigue. I could picture myself bursting out of the automatic doors onto the wet sand of my favourite beach. It still has that same power of escapism.

title: Sounds of the Summer
text:
‘You Only Live Once’ – The Strokes
This is one of my favourite songs by The Strokes, and that is a very difficult choice to make. There are few other artists that can make you feel cool in the way The Strokes can, like sunglasses, open-top car down an open road in the summer heat.

title: Sounds of the Summer
text:
‘End of August’ – Noah Kahan
A fitting song to end the list, ‘End of August’ is a homage to the end of a long summer, the twilight days when the warmth is behind you, the fields are the colour of straw and the last lazy days of August are buried underneath suncream and sprinklers. There is something beautifully melancholy about this song, as it ushers in not only autumn but a premature winter. Against the background of cicadas, you can imagine yourself sat on a flimsy, dirty plastic chair as the sun sets, the bugs swarming around your ankles, a drink in hand, the heat finally giving way to the temperamental evening breeze. Already, you can feel the promise of another summer, another year, another love, another life.

title: Desert Island Disks
text:
‘Downtown’ - Majical Cloudz
I would be hard pressed to find a song that means quite as much to me as this one. ‘Downtown’ is by far my most listened to track, racking up over two thousand listens since I discovered it just under ten years ago. I was first introduced to the song through one of my favourite shows, Brit Marling’s The OA (2016), which I remember vividly watching over and over in the summer following the end of my GCSE exams. The scene in which ‘Downtown’ features is one which requires a whole red-string board of explanation, so I won’t try to unravel that here.
‘Downtown’ is a melancholy, hypnotic ballad which immediately sunk its claws into me and has refused to budge ever since. It has a rare power that I have not found in any other songs: it has grown with me, capturing my sense of being both at sixteen and twenty-five. This is the song that I show to people when I want them to know me. It is both love and heartbreak, comfort and loneliness.

title: Desert Island Disks
text:
‘With or Without You’ - U2
I don’t remember the first time I heard U2’s iconic single ‘With Or Without You’. I was probably so young that it passed unnoticed into the background of my life, carrying with it a steady stream of memories into my adult life. Bono is a juggernaut in this song, it’s one of U2’s biggest hits for a reason. The only way I can describe his voice is transcendent. If I listen to this song alone at night I can feel almost as if I’ve cheated death. It’s a beautiful and painful depiction of a troubled relationship. And the melody is just so damn good.

title: Desert Island Disks
text:
‘My Kind of Woman’ - Mac DeMarco
This is by far the newest addition to the list. I discovered this song only at the start of 2026, a few days before New Year. In the span of a few days of travelling to Norway, I had managed to rack up over 600 listens (it helped that I had the 14-hour journey from hell there and back again). The first chord lassoed me with the grip of a noose and every time I listen it never loses its shine. It is a difficult decision to rate a song so high when I have only known it for half a year, but you know what they say: when you know, you know.
One thing I love about ‘My Kind of Woman’ is the artful panning (stereophonic sound playing different melodies and rhythms in each headphone). I can almost always be found with my trusty (for the eight-month shelf life) wired Apple headphones, and one of my favourite things to do while listening into this song is to focus in turn on the layered elements in each respective headphone. It’s a technique I’ve loved for a while, one which I first grew to adore in a near-inclusion in this list, ‘The Masterplan’ by Oasis. DeMarco somehow manages to capture just about every emotion of the last six months in this one song, from falling in love to falling apart. Even if in years to come this song loses some of its original excitement, it will still doubtlessly bring me right back here, to these months of my life.

title: Desert Island Disks
text:
‘Read My Mind’ - The Killers
It’s a big ask to name my favourite song by The Killers. I’ve been a fan since I was probably fourteen or fifteen, cemented completely in my years at sixth form college, where I have many a treasured memory of listening to their entire discography between college, home and work. However, it only takes a little relaxation of the brain for the answer to become achingly clear. It’s got to be ‘Read My Mind’, a standout single from their second album, Sam’s Town. While at a push, I would probably choose Hot Fuss for a desert island album, ‘Read My Mind’ stands out to be as one of the greatest Killers songs and one which has the most emotional pull in my life.
It’s the bridge that really captures me. I remember being obsessed with it while writing my first full-length novel (which has since been shelved and will likely never see the light of day). I love the music video, which features the band members roving around Tokyo. I love the instrumentals, I love the lyrics (‘slippin’ in my faith until I fall’ is simply brilliant), I love the beautiful sense of scale and the Springsteen-esque vibe. It’s simply a classic to me.

title: Desert Island Disks
text:
‘No 1 Party Anthem’ - Arctic Monkeys
Although these aren’t ranked in order, I think it’s fitting to round off this list with Arctic Monkeys’ ‘No 1 Party Anthem’. It’s the last song at the party, it’s collecting the rubbish at the end of the night and wondering where it all went wrong. This song could make me cry. It’s haunting in more ways than one, and there are years of my life that are lost within its hypnotic melody. It’s not a love song, rather far from it, which is once again fitting for the period of my life I associate it with.
Again, the bridge seals the deal. It is the feeling of looking across the room at someone and knowing you have to let them go. In my opinion, it’s AM at their finest, no notes. I’ve spent many an afternoon perfecting a music video for this song in my mind, daydreaming about an opportunity to direct it for myself one day. Increasingly it looks unlikely, but that doesn’t stop me entertaining it. It’s a good way to round off this list, the moment it ends you think ‘yeah, time to head home.’

title: Red, White and Blue Kites
text:
It’s hard to distinguish the bright copper of a Red Kite’s coat in this photograph, taken as it was with the incorrect lens, over the bright skies of Elan Valley on a cold day in March. A quick search and I could find a vastly superior picture, but I am adamant on only using my own photographs for these short blog posts, so this is the best I can give. There’s no doubt it’s a Red Kite though, with the impressive wingspan and dark wing tips. Its tail is a little less forked than some, but I’m comforted in my assertion by the identification of its call, a thin piping, by the Merlin app. I know that it’s not completely accurate, but it is certainly still a league ahead of my current ornithology knowledge. This is something that I’m working on, however. It is a fun pastime to identify birds not only by their appearance but also their call. My memory generally betrays me, but I hope that repetition and practice will prove fruitful.
It is a comfort to drive along motorways and notice how prevalent birds of prey are becoming in the UK. When I was young, I may see a bird of prey a few times a year, and it was a spectacular event. Now, on a long drive, I’ve been known to see up to seven or eight in a single trip. Red Kites (Milvus milvus) are scavenger birds. They feed mostly on carrion, roadkill and worms, occasionally catching small live prey. They are a common sight circling above roads, farms and woodland. They have an average lifespan of four years and are classified as Green in conservation status. While they are now a protected species, they were once hunted close to extinction in the UK, due to their perceived threat to game birds and domestic animals. Indeed, at points, they carried a sullied reputation as sly scavengers of rubbish, with the line ‘when the kite builds, look to your lesser linen’ referencing the theft of washing for nesting season in Shakespeare’s King Lear. In the mid-15th century in Scotland, King James II ordered for the Red Kite population to be killed wherever possible, and they were also included in Tudor ‘vermin laws’ and were often the target for egg collectors. In the 1980s, they were one of three globally threatened species in the UK. Now, they are a conservation success story, reintroduced across the last thirty years. In 1990, thirteen birds (two Welsh and eleven Spanish) were released in the Chilterns, on the Oxfordshire/Buckinghamshire border, and have since successfully bred in the wild and expanded across the UK.
It was a pleasure to see this one in Wales, its native land. What to say about these magnificent birds? They seem to have briefly fallen to the same fate as other wild animals that feed on carrion, the most recognisable being vultures, whose name is synonymous with greed and cruelty. Vultures, while a little shocking to look at, are nature’s clean-up crew, using their powerful stomach acid to safely digest diseased meat. We could liken it to the cooption of ‘pig’ for a gluttonous, rude and dirty person, when pigs themselves are clean and intelligent. It can be difficult not to impose human values on animals, to understand their traits and behaviour as a reflection of our own, or to hunt for morality in instinct and biology. Perhaps we abhor any signs of primitivism in ourselves, rejecting the savage and untamed, when we are only animals who read and write and build machines to drive and destroy. The Red Kite in the sky over Elan Valley was hunting for something just as I was. Its keen eyes could likely see better than my camera lens could. If I could swap places for a moment, open my great wingspan on that cold, clear day in March, and arch down to the open valley, a great fissure in the earth, I would land somewhere quiet, where no human voices could be found, no music or laughter. To break the silence there would only be a simpler song, sung by the ancestors of dinosaurs, of the days before and the days after, of the absence of the rule of man.

title: Laverstock Hill in Bloom
text:
I spent many afternoons during my school years up Laverstock Hill. Although I have not visited in a while, it is still warmly wrapped up in nostalgia, the soft blanket of childhood memory. I have videos and photographs of rolling down the grassy dunes of the field behind my school, of the herd of cows that roved intermittently across the downs, of the swing fashioned from old rope and a plank of wood that sat overlooking the city. In PE, they made us run up and back down the hill for cross country. The yearly ‘mini marathon’ was a mile-round trip of the muddy, trodden paths up to the hill. It has been a while since I’ve done that walk, years, but I can still remember the route like the back of my hand, could do it blindfolded, even. In those memories, I recall a very straightforward time, my life regimented by timetables and lunches and GCSE exams. Yet, they were also the careless years, the years before pretending, when I was old enough to know who I was but still young enough not to question it. Who could hold their handstand for the longest? How do I get out of this year’s Sports Day? Whose house for a sleepover?
These photos are from the last time I walked the route in its entirety, in June of 2020, the peak of Britain’s COVID-19 lockdown. I walked it alone, listened to a few good songs, walked almost directly in the footsteps of myself at fifteen, twelve, seven. It’s still as beautiful as it was then. I start with ‘Wildfire’ by Seafret and end with ‘Getaway’ by Blossoms. These songs too are relics now, almost six years since they were on repeat in all my playlists. I used to have a habit of taking photos of my screen with my Lumix bridge camera, an ‘artsy’ way of flexing my music taste to my 63 followers on Instagram. While writing this, I thought to search Laverstock Hill up online, expecting perhaps a description of the nature or geological structure, but I found nothing. A short article from the Salisbury Journal recounting a similar experience of walking up and viewing the city from the ‘summit’, written in 2010. Laverstock Hill is not a spectacular formation, it is not a noteworthy landscape, and yet to me it has inscribed so many years of my life that it may as well be as important as Ben Nevis or Kilimanjaro. Of course, I jest. But then again, maybe I don’t. We leave ourselves all over the landscape; a place is never just a place.

title: (Still) Life
text:
I have never been the biggest fan of still life paintings. In my “local” museum, Cambridge’s Fitzwilliam, the first room in the upstairs gallery is a self-proclaimed “Flower Room”, the walls lined from floor to ceiling with technically impeccable depictions of flower vases. I have always liked this room, largely for the overall impression it gives, the way you can lose yourself in the uniformity and simplicity. Take a closer look, however, and I’m almost immediately bored. All the paintings look the same. While their technique and skill are faultless, these painting don’t make me feel very much, and what’s the point of art if it doesn’t make you feel, right?

We painted a lot of still life in school for this very purpose: it develops important skills within a controlled environment, that allows an artist to develop their understanding of several important aspects of painting. As the artist, you set up the composition, meaning that you decide on the light, the objects, the difficulty, as well as creating through the image a narrative, theme or colour harmony. Still life is not a simple snapshot of some objects lying around, it is often carefully orchestrated, it can mean something just as a portrait might. Some still life paintings worth mentioning are Paul Cezanne’s Still Life with Sugar, Caravaggio’s Basket of Fruit, Vincent Van Gogh’s Sunflowers and John Singer Sargent’s Roses. I’ll focus on each in turn. Cezanne’s Still Life carries with it a distinct sense of movement beyond the frame, the tablecloth is rumpled beneath the fruit, the scene feels rushed and quite technically inaccurate in terms of its use of perspective. It is an impression fit for a (post)impressionist. Caravaggio is, in contrast, far more technically accurate. His level of detail is immaculate, if a little harshly defined against the plain background. This reminds me of the flower paintings, although I do feel a twinge of something looking at it, an admiration of the Baroque perfection, perhaps. Sunflowers needs no further introduction. If you were ever to feel something looking at a still life, you would feel it with this. What makes Sunflowers so compelling is not just the fact that we know the artist (as Van Gogh’s own life and history are doubtlessly a powerful emotional pull to his paintings), but it is that we feel as if we truly know the subject. When I look at this painting, I can see the moment it’s captured, the flowers that will doubtlessly shrivel and die beyond the frame, engendering a melancholy beauty to their proud heads. Sargent’s Roses are just a step beyond. The beautifully composed handful of roses lie on the edge of a desk, they are almost decaying before our eyes.
There, then, is the beauty I have found in still life. For a moment, they stop time, they stop decay, they stop life. They exist in a moment where the flower is forever in bloom, the plum always ripe, the apple always browning. All those flowers in the Fitzwilliam died a very long time ago, and every time a curious visitor steps into Gallery 17, they are born again.

The paintings throughout this article are attempts of still life from a holiday in Wales in 2025. They are not technically admirable, rely far more on bold colour and contrast than they do on meaning or vision. They are painted with gouache, each completed within a two-hour period (the time it takes to watch a film) and inspired not by objects before me, but rather hastily found Pinterest pics. They did, however, give me a little taste of still life splendour, provided a drive to try more, to compose my own images, and to depict life even when it’s standing still.
